copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice. The Bay Area leans Operate, with two public ferry operators today and the most proven Enable precedents of any market.
copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing terminals and marina berths and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; the ask is access, not money. The Port of San Francisco already licenses private water-taxi operators on its docks — this pathway exists here today.
copy.operate_track: The Bay's public bodies already own ferry fleets, procure zero-emission vessels, and operate routes. Navier vessels can be procured the way transit vessels are already procured here — to build, run, or augment the public water network.

copy.headline: Your speed rules were written for boats that make wake.
copy.framing: Open Bay water carries no numeric speed cap for a vessel of this class — this network's base schedules already run at full foiling speed legally. The binding rules are marina-basin and channel rules written to control wake and protect people near docks.
copy.ask: Our ask is narrow: measure us. In the estuary and channel reaches where a posted rule's purpose is wake control, grant marked-channel transit speeds where independent wake and noise measurement shows that purpose is served.

_provenance.structure: Narrower relief case than Boston per SPEED-RULES-BAY-AREA.md §4: California HNC §655.2 is proximity/safety-triggered (no relief claimed where the rule protects people); the RNA 15-kn cap is tonnage-gated at 1,600 GT (does not bind an N45); relief is relevant only in the Oakland Estuary (BA-3/BA-4) and Sausalito Channel (BA-2) reaches, via local marine-enforcement authorities where the rule is wake-purposed (posted no-wake zones; RBRA Ordinance 91-1).

rule_basis.detail: 5 mph within 100 ft of a bather and 200 ft of bathing beaches, swim floats, and passenger landing floats, where not locally regulated
5 mph limit in the Sausalito Channel; due caution at all times in the harbor
15-kn cap gated at 1,600 GT — far above an N45; precautionary-area caution duty applies to all vessels

rule_basis.instrument: Alameda marine enforcement (HNC §655.2(a)(2) + posted NO WAKE zones)
rule_basis.detail: no vessel over 5 mph within 200 ft of any floating dock or marina; off-plane and fully settled in posted no-wake zones

_provenance.base_times_policy: hub.json water_min values stand as base; 5-mph zones bind only near landings/basins (inside dwell allowance) except the Oakland Estuary and Sausalito Channel reaches, where displacement-speed transit is assumed. No exemption assumed anywhere in base UI. Carried by fn5.

expander.title: What speed-rule relief unlocks
body: Most of this network already runs at full speed legally: open Bay water has no numeric cap for a vessel of this class, and the five-mph rules bind only close to docks, swimmers and landings — moments already inside every schedule.

Two reaches are different: the Oakland Estuary and the Sausalito Channel, where five-mph and no-wake zones extend beyond the berth. Where a rule's purpose is wake control, a foiling vessel serves that purpose at speed — our ask is independent wake and noise measurement, then marked-channel transit speeds through the mechanisms local marine-enforcement authorities already hold.
Where a rule protects people near the water rather than property from wake, we do not ask for relief.
Indicative scale if estuary and channel relief were granted: roughly two to four minutes per affected leg — shown only here, as what relief could unlock, never in base schedules.
Precedent: Stockholm's public transport authority runs an electric hydrofoil ferry at roughly twice the posted zone speed under a low-wake exemption.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 30 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: The Bay Area's water-transportation landscape spans regional, port, and municipal bodies. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Regional public transit agency; owns vessels, procures zero-emission newbuilds, operates routes serving five cities, and leads expansion studies at Mission Bay, Berkeley, Redwood City and South San Francisco.

bodies.body: Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District
bodies.role: Operates Golden Gate Ferry to Larkspur, Sausalito and Tiburon; owns the Larkspur terminal and operates the Sausalito terminal on city-leased land.
City port authority for the SF waterfront; owns South Beach Harbor, co-leads the Mission Bay Ferry Landing, and already licenses private water-taxi operators on its docks.
Owns Jack London Square, home of the Oakland Ferry Terminal.
City-chartered port whose commission controls the marina and waterfront; actively partnering on design and permitting for a permanent ferry landing.

bodies.body: BCDC — SF Bay Conservation and Development Commission
bodies.role: Regulates fill, dredging and shoreline development Bay-wide; any new float, gangway or dock modification at any station runs through a BCDC permit.
The nine-county region's transportation planning and financing agency; Regional Measure 3 funds are a named source for ferry expansion and electric vessels.

bodies.body: City of South San Francisco + San Mateo County Harbor District
bodies.role: The city owns the Oyster Point Marina land; the Harbor District operates the marina, alongside the public ferry terminal on site.
San Francisco's transportation agency; the T-Third light rail runs one block from the Mission Bay Ferry Landing — the landside half of that interchange.
Owns and operates Berkeley Marina berthing; a public Berkeley ferry study is under way, and the city has hosted private commuter ferry service before.
Owns the ferry-terminal land, leased long-term to the Golden Gate district.
City authority for Treasure Island, where a privately funded commuter ferry already runs to the Ferry Building — proof of privately financed service in this market.
